STATEMENT OF INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE1
Amici curiae are family members of children and
educators killed in the Sandy Hook Elementary School
Shooting on December 14, 2012.
Amici Carlee Soto Parisi, Jillian Soto-Marino, and
Carlos Mathew Soto are the siblings of first-grade teacher
Victoria Leigh Soto. Amica Do nna So to is Vi cki So to ’ s
mother.
Amici Jacqueline and Mark Barden are the parents
of first-grader Daniel Gerard Barden.
Amica Jennifer Hensel is the mother of first-grader
Avielle Rose Richman. Avielle’s father is deceased.
Amici Alissa and Robert Parker are the parents of
first-grader Emilie Alice Parker.
Amici Nicole and Ian Hockley are the parents of firstgrader Dylan Christopher Jack Hockley.
Amici David and Francine Wheeler are the parents
of first-grader Benjamin Andrew Wheeler.
1. Pursuant to Supreme Court Rule 37.6, amici curiae
certify that a party’s counsel did not author this brief in whole
or in part; a party or a party’s counsel did not contribute money
that was intended to fund preparing or submitting the brief;
and no person–other than the above-listed amici curiae  or their
counsel–contributed money that was intended to fund preparing
or submitting the brief.

2
The assault on Sandy Hook Elementary School,
carried out by an untrained, 112-pound youth armed
with an AR-15-style rifle, is graphic proof of the unusual
and extreme lethality of that firearm and the harm it is
capable of inflicting on American communities. Amici
seek to protect other American families from becoming
casualties in another AR-15 killing spree. Restrictions
on these weapons are constitutionally appropriate and
crucial to that purpose.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
 The right to bear arms is not a right “to keep and
carry any weapon whatsoever.” Dist. of Columbia v.
Heller, 554 U.S. 570, 626–27 (2008). It is limited by the
historical tradition prohibiting “the carrying of dangerous
and unusual weapons.” Id. at 627. A state’s legislature
may restrict possession of unusually dangerous weapons
that wreak excessive, lethal harm on the public. See
United States v. Rahimi , 602 U.S. 680, 691, 698 (2024).
The AR-15-style rifle is such a weapon and is accordingly
appropriately restricted by Conn. Gen. Stats. §§ 53-202a
et seq. and other similar enactments, such as Cook County,
Ill. Code § 54-212(a).
The AR-15-style rifle that enabled the shooter to kill
twenty-six people in under five minutes at Sandy Hook
Elementary School was purchased legally. In the aftermath
of the shooting, the twenty-six lives taken at Sandy Hook
Elementary School could not be restored. The faith of a
community and a state in its peace and security could not
be re-made. But the state’s legislature could and did take
appropriate measures to protect Connecticut’s citizens
from future AR-15 attacks by enacting restrictions on

3
that unusually and extremely lethal firearm. Connecticut’s
restrictions on these weapons, Conn. Gen. Stats. §§ 53-
202a et seq., recognize and respond to the unusual and
extreme dangers they pose.
ARGUMENT
THE AR-15 IS UNUSUALLY
AND EXTREMELY LETHAL
The Armalite 15 rifle was made for the battlefield.
Its design harnesses technology to obliterate enemy
combatants. Easy to use and light-weight, the AR-15 has
a barrel designed for high muzzle velocity and deadly
accuracy, low-recoil semi-automatic fire capability, and the
ability to accept a 30-round or higher external magazine
of relatively small and lightweight bullets that themselves
are engineered for extreme velocity and lethality. 2 These
design features combine to create the battlefield virtues
of “phenomenal lethality,” “increased ability to penetrate
helmets and body armor” and “engineer[ing] to generate
maximum wound effect.” 3 Semi-automatic fire mode—a
design feature the AR-15 shares with the M-16—confers
another battlefield advantage: it is “the most important
firing technique during fast-moving modern combat.” 4
Teamed with large capacity magazines, fired in semi-

And that is before yet speaking of the effect rounds
projected from an AR-15-style rifle have on the human

effects of those bullets are more lethal. Instead of being
hit by just one bullet, the body is hit with three, and each
wound alone would kill. 6 The impact on the small bodies
of children at Sandy Hook is documented. 7

5
It is sometimes argued that AR-15-style rifles sold
for civilian use are safer than M-16s because civilianmarket AR-15-style rifles do not have an automatic fire
mode. That is not so. The Army’s own Field Manual states
that semi-automatic fire is the “most important firing
technique during fast-moving, modern combat,” and notes
that “[i]t is surprising how devastatingly accurate rapid
semi-automatic fire can be.” 8 Saying that the AR-15’s
extreme lethality is meaningfully diminished because it
does not have fully automatic capacity “is like saying that
a conventional bomber is not a war plane because it isn’t
carrying a nuclear payload.” 9
The widespread availability of AR-15-style rifles
has had catastrophic effects on public safety in America.
“[W]ith the invention and commercial availability of new
technologies that gave individuals or small groups of
people the power to kill large number of people in a short
amount of time,” the “character of mass murder began to
change.”10 There is “a growing preference for using assault
weapons and large capacity magazines” to perpetrate
attacks, particularly in high-fatality mass shootings.11 Our
children are all too often the targets of these attacks. Not
only is the frequency of mass shootings rising in America,
the frequency of mass shootings in schools is rising. 12

6
The urge to violence has existed throughout human
history. One of the things that has restrained it is the
physical difficulty of killing another human. Assault
weapon technology all but eliminates that physical
difficulty—and that is precisely why it is appropriately
restricted by Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 53-202a et seq., and Cook
County, Ill. Code § 54-212(a).
I. THE SANDY HOOK SHOOTER’S LEGAL
ACCESS TO AN AR-15-STYLE RIFLE ENABLED
HIM TO KILL TWENTY CHILDREN AND SIX
EDUCATORS IN UNDER FIVE MINUTES
For his assault on Sandy Hook Elementary School
the Sandy Hook shooter chose a Bushmaster AR-15,
the XM15-E2S. 13 The weapon was legally purchased in
13. This was the same model weapon that had been used in

of Columbia, Maryland and Virginia in 2002, a decade before
Sandy Hook. See Fox Butterfield, Sniper Victims in Settlement

McWhirter & Sadie Gurman, Accused Buffalo Gunman Described
Why He Chose His Firearms, Body Armor , The Wall Street
Journal (May 16, 2022), https://www.wsj.com/livecoverage/

Connecticut.14 Despite the lethality of AR-15-style rifles
and large capacity magazines, Connecticut’s then-existing
assault weapons restrictions permitted the sale of the
Bushmaster XM15-E2S and the 5.56 mm rounds15 housed
in 30-round magazines that the shooter would use. 16 If
Connecticut’s now-operative assault weapons restrictions
had been in effect at that time, those sales would not have
taken place.17
 The shooter had no military or police weapons
training.18 He was not physically strong. At six feet tall,
he weighed 112 pounds. 19 B u t  arm e d  wi th  th e  AR- 1 5,
large capacity magazines, and attack tactics learned
through first-person shooter games, he unleashed torrents

manufacturer, he made the “[f]orces of opposition ... bow
down.”21 He inflicted killing wounds on twenty children
and six educators in just 264 seconds. 22 Had the shooter
been carrying another firearm, he would not have been
able to so easily carry, load, and fire so many well-aimed
5.56 mm rounds in so short a time—and amici’s loved ones
could be alive today. The lethal prowess of the weapon he
carried made Sandy Hook the historic tragedy that it is.23
The mass loss of life caused by an amateur shooter
with an AR-15-style rifle at Sandy Hook Elementary
School was no accident. The result at Sandy Hook is
exactly what the AR-15’s field testing predicted. Mass
shootings since Sandy Hook repeat the proof. On May
24, 2022 in Uvalde, Texas, a young male shooter with
no combat training used an AR-15-style rifle and large
capacity magazines to kill 19 students and two teachers

During his assault on Sandy Hook Elementary School,
the shooter used only one weapon—the Bushmaster AR-

using thirty-round magazines in taped reloads to reduce

In the words of Nicole Hockley, the mother of firstgrader Dylan:
There were a lot of guns that our shooter could
have chosen. He chose the AR-15 because he
was aware of how many shots it could get out…
that it would serve his objective of killing as
many people as possible in the shortest time
possible.
II. NO ONE CAN BRING BACK THOSE LOST AT
SANDY HOOK
There were twenty-six lives taken on December 14,
2012 at Sandy Hook Elementary School.

11
Victoria Soto
Victoria Leigh Soto was 27 on December 14, 2012,
and the first-grade teacher in Sandy Hook Elementary
School’s Classroom 10.
Vicki had known she wanted to be a teacher since
she was three years old. She worked hard to get there.
Attending Eastern Connecticut State University in
Willimantic, she excelled and graduated with a double
major in history and education. Vicki was the oldest of
the four Soto children, a role model to her two younger
sisters and her brother.
E v e ry  y e ar  Vi c ki  h ad  b i g  p l an s  f o r  s e t tin g  u p  h e r
classroom to welcome her new students. In what became
a family tradition, she would enlist her siblings to help
change the bulletin boards and arrange her classroom

12
in fun and engaging ways. Her enthusiasm only grew as
school got rolling. She would sit with her mom, Donna,
on the patio cutting out letters and talking about each of
her students.
That morning on the long drive from her home in
Stratford, Vicki was blasting Christmas music. She was
bringing in all the ingredients so her class could make
gingerbread houses for the holidays.
Vicki died trying to protect her students.

13
Daniel Barden
Daniel Barden was—at age 7—one of the older children
in Sandy Hook Elementary School’s Classroom 8. Daniel
understood things about life in a way that prompted many
who knew him to call him an “old soul.” He was not only
bright and loving, he understood what it meant to live life with
compassion. He would take notice of children who sat alone and
would ask to go sit with them or invite them to join an activity.
Daniel was the baby of the family, growing up in a
happy little house. He got a lot of attention from his two
older siblings. He giggled with his older brother and sister,
keeping small secrets from their parents.
On the morning of the shooting, Daniel walked to the
bus with his father Mark. They were talking about how
they would have pizza that night, because Friday night was
family pizza night. It was going to be a great Friday night.

14
Mark put Daniel on the bus and hugged him and kissed
him and told him he loved him. He had no way of knowing
it would be the last time.

15
Dylan Hockley
Dylan Hockley was six. He had a beaming smile that
lit up a room and an infectious laugh. His older brother was
his best friend. Dylan loved the moon, and garlic bread,
and being right next to his mom, Nicole.
Dylan was a child with autism and was learning to
read. He would come home every day from school proudly
bearing a new book. One of the main reasons the Hockley
family moved to Sandy Hook was the school’s special
education program. Dylan’s parents had chosen Sandy
Hook Elementary School for Dylan because there was
a strong focus on special education needs and Newtown
could provide the staff and the services and the expertise
to help Dylan.

16
The last time Dylan’s father, Ian, saw him was the
morning of December 14th. Ian had to be at work by seven,
so he got up very early. He looked in the boys’ room. They
were asleep, so Ian whispered goodbye and went to work.

17
Avielle Richman
On the morning of December 14, 2012, Avielle
Richman had plans to leave school early with her family
and go see the Rockettes perform. Avielle wasn’t supposed
to be in school at all that day, but she really wanted to
build gingerbread houses with her class. Avielle’s mom
Jenn says “this girl had crazy, crazy curly hair and she
had her father’s smile; just half of her face was this smile,
just like his. She was not at all shy…” Avielle was a lover
of stories—both hearing them and telling them. “She was
our only child, she was everything.”
On the morning of the shooting, Jenn took Avielle
to the bus. She got on and they blew kisses through the
window to each other.

18
Jenn says:
I don’t think you heal from something like this.
I think you forever hold grief and you rebuild
some joy back into your life, and it balances.
And some days, on other days, one takes over
the other and the other days the grief is just
so awful.

19
Emilie Parker
On December 14, 2012, Emilie Parker woke up early,
like she usually did. She waited until 7 a.m. to get out of
her bed because that was the family rule. When her father
Robbie poked his head into her room before leaving for
work, she smiled and they exchanged good-mornings and
I-love-yous in Portuguese, a language Emilie was learning
from her dad. She had begged him to teach her.
Emilie’s parents felt that she was this amazing glue
and bond in their home. Each person had their unique
relationship with her, including her two younger sisters.
She loved to draw and paint and wanted to open an art
gallery when she grew up.
On the morning of the shooting, Emilie’s mother,
Alissa, took her to the bus. They had a family tradition
that when the kids got on the bus, they would all turn
around and wave goodbye. But that morning was rushed,

20
and Alissa had to help another child. Emilie ran over and
gave Alissa a hug and got on the bus. She didn’t turn
around and wave. Alissa stood there waving, waiting for
her to turn and wave back, and she didn’t. That was the
last time Alissa saw Emilie.

21
Benjamin Wheeler
On the morning of December 14, 2012, Benjamin
Wheeler, 6, wasn’t sure if he wanted to be an architect, a
paleontologist, a lighthouse keeper—or all three at once.
Ben was an avid reader and was becoming a very strong
swimmer. He really hated the fact that he “was already 6
and hadn’t lost any teeth.” Each morning Ben could hardly
wait to get to Classroom 8.
On the morning of the shooting, Ben’s mother,
Francine, drove him to school. It was about 9 o’clock and
Ben was so excited to go into school that he left the car
door open. Francine told him to close the door. She doesn’t
remember if she said I love you, she just remembers saying
close the door. She says, “That was the last thing I said
to him, and then he went in.”

22
III. THERE SHOULD BE NO NEXT TIME
In the words of amica Nicole Hockley, “I do not want
to be someone sharing my experience and consoling
another parent next time. I do not want there to be a
next time.”
In the words of amicus Ian Hockley,
I speak for our dead son Dylan, who never
stood a chance as he stared down the barrel of
a military grade weapon. I cannot bring Dylan
back, but together we must try to avoid the next
mass shooting using these weapons and prevent
many more families suffering the horrors we
experienced.
In the words of amicus Mathew Soto,
An assault weapons ban would have saved my
sister Victoria Soto. The AR-15 used in the
Sandy Hook School Shooting should not have
been sold to the public. This piece of legislation
has and will continue to save lives in the state
of Connecticut. These weapons were created
for military use and still serve our military
and law enforcement; they should not be sold
to the public.
In the words of amicus  D a vi d  Wh e e l e r ,  “I  w o ul d
respectfully request that every parent in this country
who hears these words simply pause for a moment and
think. Ask yourself, what is it worth doing to keep your
children safe?”

23
In the words of amica Jillian Soto-Marino:
The Connecticut assault weapon ban is vital in
ensuring that what happened to my sister never
happens to another family again. The repeal of
this legislation would strip back what my family
as well as countless others who have lost loved
ones worked to accomplish.
In the words of amica Jackie Barden, “We know the
price of inaction.”
In the words of amicus Mark Barden, “No one should
feel the pain.  No one should feel our pain or the pain felt
by the tens of thousands of people who’ve lost loved ones
to senseless gun violence.”
In the words of amica Jennifer Hensel:
A moral imperative is truly at hand. My child
died in the arms of Connecticut’s purview; her
blood pooling on the floor of her first-grade
classroom. Her life was ended by multiple
